The Naked Bike: Touring's Underrated Hero

Ask most riders what makes a touring bike and they picture a fairing, panniers and a big screen. Yet some of my most memorable trips around Britain have been on a naked roadster: light, punchy, endlessly flickable, and honest in a way faired bikes are not. The Kawasaki Z650 and its ilk are brilliant B-road weapons that, with a handful of sensible additions, make genuinely capable tourers. The catch, and it is a big one, is the wind. Solve that and everything else falls into place.

Wind: The One Problem You Must Address

A naked bike puts you square in the airflow. At 40mph it feels wonderful, a rush of open-air freedom. At a sustained 70mph on the M6 heading north it becomes a wall of pressure that drags on your shoulders, strains your neck and leaves you shattered after an hour. This constant windblast is the number one reason naked riders give up on distance, and it is entirely fixable.

A small flyscreen or sport screen takes the blast off your chest and lifts it towards your helmet. I fit a Puig Naked New Generation Sport Screen, which is a neat bolt-on for most popular roadsters and makes a genuine difference at motorway speed. It will not give you the still-air pocket of a full tourer, but it moves the pressure off your torso and lets you relax your grip. Sizing is everything with a naked bike screen, so work through our motorcycle windscreen guide to match screen height to your torso before spending money.

Manage the wind and a naked bike stops being tiring. Ignore it and no amount of comfort kit elsewhere will save your day.

Luggage: Better Than You Think

Naked bikes generally have a usable subframe and pillion grab rails, which gives you far more luggage options than a sportsbike. You can fit proper soft panniers, a tank bag and a tail pack without exotic mounts.

  • Soft panniers such as the SW-Motech Blaze Saddlebags hang over a support frame and give you real carrying capacity without drilling the bike.
  • A tank bag like the Givi Tanklock Tank Bag keeps your wallet, phone and snacks to hand, and the Tanklock ring makes it a click on, click off affair.
  • A tail pack handles the bulky soft items and roll-mats if you are camping.

For fitting frames, weight limits and keeping bags off your exhaust and paint, our luggage mounting guide covers the practical detail. A naked bike will comfortably carry enough for a week without ever feeling overloaded.

Comfort and Long Days

The upright riding position of a naked bike is its comfort trump card. Your weight sits on your backside and your wrists stay relaxed, which is the opposite of a sportsbike and far kinder over a long day. That upright stance is why a roadster can genuinely rival dedicated tourers on twisty routes such as the A82 through Glencoe or the passes of the Lake District, where you are working the bars constantly and want to sit up and see the view.

The two things I always add are heated grips and an intercom. Oxford Heaterz Premium Heated Grips keep your hands working on a cold Welsh morning over the A44, and a Cardo Packtalk Edge Intercom lets me follow sat-nav prompts, take calls at stops and chat to riding mates on a group tour without stopping. On a naked bike, where wind noise is higher, a good intercom with wind reduction is worth every penny.

Range and Fuel Strategy

Middleweight nakeds tend to be frugal and carry a reasonable tank, so range is rarely the headache it is on a supersport. A Z650 will happily see 170 to 200 miles between fills at a touring pace. That said, upright riders sitting in the wind burn fuel faster the harder they push into the breeze, so easing your speed on exposed motorway sections helps both economy and comfort. In remote areas like the far north of the NC500, still fill up whenever you pass a station, because a comfortable range on paper means nothing if the only pump for 40 miles is closed.

Pace and Route Planning

Play to the naked bike's strengths. It is a scalpel on twisty roads and a joy on flowing A and B-roads, so build your days around Britain's great riding routes rather than motorway transits. A naked bike will happily string together the Cat and Fiddle, the Snake Pass and a loop of the Peaks, or tackle the Welsh A5 through Snowdonia, and leave you wanting more. When you must do motorway miles, break them into short stints, use your screen, and accept a slightly slower cruising speed to keep the windblast manageable.

What to Upgrade First

Spend your money in this order: screen, heated grips, soft luggage, intercom. The screen tackles the fundamental weakness, the grips and intercom make long days pleasant, and the luggage lets you actually carry your kit. None of it is expensive relative to buying a dedicated tourer, which is the whole appeal.

Honest Limitations

A naked bike will never offer the weather protection of a full-dress tourer. Sustained high-speed motorway work remains its weakest area even with a screen, and heavy rain into the chest is unavoidable. Pillion comfort is decent on a mid-size naked but not luxurious, and if you tour two-up regularly you should read our pillion touring guide to set the bike up correctly.

Who It Suits

A naked bike suits the rider who loves back-road touring, values light weight and agility, and is willing to make peace with the wind in exchange for one of the most engaging ways to see the country. The Z650 is a superb example, and its faired sibling the Kawasaki Ninja 650 is worth a look if you want the same friendly character with more built-in wind protection. For a rider building their first real touring setup on a budget, a well-sorted naked is one of the smartest choices out there, and it pairs beautifully with the picks in our best touring bikes guide.
